passage: Four puppies had been born under the stairs of B-block, and their mother looked thin. Kunal, eleven, noticed first. He didn't wait for an adult to decide. He made a chart on the back of an old calendar: who brings water, who brings leftover rice, who checks the puppies after school. Six children signed up. Vijay, the watchman, said, "Don't let them into the lift." Kunal added that to the chart too. By the end of the week the puppies were rounder, and the chart had a seventh name.

qa.q: Where were the puppies born?
qa.a: Under the stairs of B-block.

qa.q: What might Kunal have felt when the chart got a seventh name?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and encouraged that more children were joining in.

qa.q: What would help Kunal keep this going safely?
qa.a: Ask an adult to help contact an animal welfare group, so the puppies can be checked and cared for properly.

qa.q: How might Vijay see the children's plan?
qa.a: He probably appreciates it but wants it kept orderly, which is why he added the lift rule.

grounding: Shows a child taking active responsibility for caring for animals and organising others in his colony.

passage:
"Ritu, give me your bag," said Chaitanya.
"I can carry it."
"With one arm in plaster? No. I'm your buddy this month anyway."
"Ma'am made you buddy?"
"I asked her." He swung the bag onto his shoulder. "I'll write your notes too, till your arm's better."
"Your handwriting's terrible."
"Then I'll write slowly." Chaitanya, ten, held the classroom door with his foot.
"Why are you doing all this?"
He shrugged. "You'd do it if I broke my arm."
Ritu smiled. "Fine. But I'm checking the spelling."

qa.q: What did Chaitanya offer to write for Ritu?
qa.a: Her notes.

qa.q: Why might Chaitanya have asked the teacher to be Ritu's buddy?
qa.a: He felt caring and responsible, wanting to help a classmate who was struggling.

qa.q: How could the teacher support Chaitanya in this role?
qa.a: Thank him and check in with both children so the help stays useful and not overwhelming.

qa.q: How does Ritu feel about Chaitanya's help?
qa.a: She's a bit proud at first, but grateful and amused by the end.

grounding: Shows a child volunteering for a helping role and caring for an injured classmate.

passage: I'm Avni, and last year I was house captain for the school camp. On the second night, a Class 3 boy, Ujjwal, sat outside his tent crying because he missed home. The other captains were busy with the campfire. I sat with him, told him about my first camp when I also cried, and walked him to the teacher on duty so he could phone his mother. Then I stayed until he fell asleep. Being captain wasn't about the badge. It was about noticing who needed help first.

qa.q: Why was Ujjwal crying outside his tent?
qa.a: He missed home.

qa.q: What does Avni staying until Ujjwal fell asleep suggest?
qa.a: Avni felt responsible for him and caring, wanting him to feel safe.

qa.q: What did Avni get right in helping Ujjwal?
qa.a: Avni comforted him, shared a similar story and took him to the teacher on duty to call home.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal remember Avni?
qa.a: As a kind older student who made a scary night feel safe.

grounding: Shows a child in a group role taking responsibility for a homesick younger student.

passage: Rashmi, eleven, got home from school in Pune and found the door locked. Her mother Vidya was stuck at work, and Rashmi had left her key on the dining table. She felt panic rise, then remembered the steps they'd practised. Step one: don't wander. Step two: go to Mrs Iyer next door. Step three: call Mummy from Mrs Iyer's phone. Step four: wait there and do homework. She followed each one. When Vidya arrived an hour later, Rashmi was halfway through her maths.

qa.q: Where did Rashmi go after finding the door locked?
qa.a: To Mrs Iyer next door.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling when she found the door locked?
qa.a: She felt panic at first, but calmed down by remembering the steps.

qa.q: Why did the practised steps work well?
qa.a: They gave her a clear order to follow when she was scared, so she stayed safe and calm.

qa.q: How might Vidya feel when she finds Rashmi doing homework?
qa.a: Relieved and proud that Rashmi handled it sensibly.

grounding: Shows a child using practised step-by-step rules to solve being locked out safely.

passage:
"Kiran, it's your turn for dishes."
"Arohi, I have a science test tomorrow."
"I have a maths test on Thursday."
"So?"
"So let's use a rule," said Arohi, nine. "Whoever's test is first gets off chores first."
"Mine's first."
"Fine. You're off tonight. I'm off Wednesday."
"And if we both have tests the same day?"
"Then we do half each." She wrote it on the fridge whiteboard.
Kiran squinted at it. "That's actually fair."
"Rules are fair when they're the same for both."

qa.q: Where did Arohi write the rule?
qa.a: On the fridge whiteboard.

qa.q: What was Arohi thinking when she suggested a rule?
qa.a: She wanted a fair way to settle the argument, and felt confident a clear rule would work for both.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Making a rule that applies to both, because it solves this dilemma and future ones fairly.

qa.q: How does Kiran see Arohi's rule?
qa.a: He is surprised to find it fair, even though it was her idea.

grounding: Shows a child using a simple rule to settle a chore dilemma step by step.

passage: I'm Francis, and last year Sir made me cricket captain for Class 6. Fifteen boys wanted to play, and only eleven could. Pankaj, my best friend, had missed half the practices. I wanted him in. But I made myself a rule first: attendance, then catching drills, then batting scores. I wrote the list in my notebook and went down it, one by one. Pankaj came twelfth. I had to tell him. He sulked for two days, then came to every practice. This year, he's in.

qa.q: What was Francis's first rule for choosing players?
qa.a: Attendance.

qa.q: How did Francis feel about Pankaj coming twelfth?
qa.a: Francis felt torn and uncomfortable, wanting to include his friend but sticking to the fair rule.

qa.q: What would you advise Francis about telling Pankaj?
qa.a: Tell Pankaj privately and explain the rules clearly, so he knows how to get in next time.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Francis's decision now?
qa.a: Pankaj may respect it more now, since the clear rule showed him what to work on.

grounding: Shows a child using structured rules to make a hard team selection.

passage: I'm Yash, and in Class 6 I left my science project until the last night. I told myself I'd start every day for three weeks. Then the night before, I panicked. My friend Vikas messaged, "Copy mine, change the colours." I nearly did. But I thought about Sir's face if he found out, and about how I'd feel handing it in. I stayed up and made a bad one myself. It got a C. Since then I do twenty minutes every evening, even when I don't feel like it.

qa.q: What grade did Yash's project get?
qa.a: It got a C.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling the night before the project was due?
qa.a: Yash felt panicked and tempted to copy, but also uneasy about cheating.

qa.q: What would you advise Yash for the next big project?
qa.a: Break it into small daily parts from the first week, like his new twenty-minute habit.

qa.q: What might Vikas have been thinking when he offered his project?
qa.a: He probably wanted to help his friend, not realising it was dishonest.

grounding: Shows a child choosing honest work over copying after procrastinating, and building a study routine.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Kishore, November
Damini (11) has been on time every day this month, which is new for her. She now does homework in the library before the bus. During Tuesday's test, the boy beside her left his answer sheet uncovered while he went to sharpen a pencil. I saw Damini turn her paper over and look away until he returned. She got a lower mark than him, but it was her own. I've told her privately that I noticed, and I'll mention her new routine to her parents.

qa.q: What did Damini do when the boy's answer sheet was uncovered?
qa.a: She turned her paper over and looked away until he returned.

qa.q: What might Damini have felt when she saw the uncovered sheet?
qa.a: She may have been tempted but chose honesty, feeling it mattered more than the mark.

qa.q: Why was Kishore right to tell Damini privately that he noticed?
qa.a: It shows her honest choice is valued without embarrassing her in front of others.

qa.q: How might Damini's parents feel when they hear about her new routine?
qa.a: Proud and encouraged by the change in her punctuality and study habits.

grounding: Shows a child building punctuality and study routines and choosing academic honesty, noted by her teacher.

passage:
Yusuf's diary, Monday
Plan: homework at five. Reality: played cricket till seven. Then dinner. Then I was tired. My sister Farida saw my face and said, "Timer, little brother." We set it for twenty-five minutes. No talking. I did the English worksheet and half the maths. Then a five-minute break. Then the other half. Done by nine. I hate admitting it, but the timer works. Tomorrow I'm doing homework at five before cricket. I'll write in here if I actually do it.

qa.q: How long did they set the timer for?
qa.a: Twenty-five minutes.

qa.q: What does Yusuf writing "I hate admitting it" suggest?
qa.a: Yusuf felt a bit sheepish but relieved that the timer helped to stop the putting-off.

qa.q: What small step would help Yusuf tomorrow?
qa.a: Start the timer at five before going out, so cricket becomes the reward after homework.

qa.q: How might Farida see Yusuf's evening?
qa.a: Farida probably feels pleased that the timer idea helped Yusuf get it done.

grounding: Shows a child noticing a habit of procrastination and trying a simple routine to study.

passage: At the temple fair in the small town, Pranav, ten, had fifty rupees from his Nani. The plastic gun at Bhupen's stall cost forty. "It breaks in a week," said his cousin. Pranav picked it up, put it down, picked it up again. Then he walked past the stalls, comparing. A kite and a big spool of string cost thirty together. He bought them and kept twenty in his pocket. Bhupen laughed. "Thinking like a shopkeeper." That evening the kite flew higher than the neighbour's.

qa.q: How much did the plastic gun cost?
qa.a: Forty rupees.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling as he picked the gun up and put it down?
qa.a: He felt tempted but unsure whether it was worth the money.

qa.q: What would you advise Pranav about the twenty rupees left over?
qa.a: Talk with Nani or a parent about whether to save it or spend it on something he really values.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Pranav's choice?
qa.a: With amused respect, seeing a boy who compared prices carefully.

grounding: Shows a child comparing value at a fair and choosing something longer-lasting over a quick buy.

passage: In their small flat in Taipei, Mei, eleven, caught her younger brother Wei leaving the bathroom light on again. "Electricity costs money," she said, flicking it off. She had been saving her pocket money in a jar for three months for a book on birds. When her schoolbag strap broke, her mother offered a new one. Mei shook her head, found a needle and thread, and stitched it. "It works," she told Wei. "Then the money can go to the book." Wei watched her, then turned off his own lamp.

qa.q: What was Mei saving for?
qa.a: A book on birds.

qa.q: Why did Mei choose to stitch her bag instead of getting a new one?
qa.a: She felt determined and a little proud, wanting to save her money for the book she really wanted.

qa.q: What might help Mei decide when to repair and when to replace?
qa.a: Asking her mother whether the repair is safe and will last, so she can make a sensible choice.

qa.q: How might Wei see his older sister's choices?
qa.a: He seems to admire her a little, since he starts copying her by turning off his lamp.

grounding: Shows a child valuing money and resources by saving, repairing and not wasting electricity.

passage: In the school canteen, Gurleen, twelve, watched half-eaten plates of rice go into the big bin. Wasim, the canteen uncle, sighed. "Every day, a full bin." Gurleen thought of the dal her mother measured each morning. She made a sign: "Take what you'll eat. Come back for more." She stuck it above the serving counter with Wasim's permission. The first week, the bin was only half full. Wasim gave her a thumbs up. "Saved one whole pot today."

qa.q: What did Gurleen's sign say?
qa.a: "Take what you'll eat. Come back for more."

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when she watched the rice go into the bin?
qa.a: She was bothered and uneasy about the waste, thinking of how carefully her mother measured food.

qa.q: What made Gurleen's plan work?
qa.a: It was simple, she asked Wasim first, and it let students take more if they needed it.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel about the change?
qa.a: Relieved and appreciative that less food and effort were being wasted.

grounding: Shows a child noticing wasted resources in her school canteen and acting to reduce it.

passage: I'm Raghav, Zubin's classmate. At our school's Independence Day assembly, when the anthem started, most of us were shuffling or whispering. Zubin, who's eleven, stood completely still, chin up, hands at his sides. After the anthem, the wind blew one of the small paper flags off the stage. Zubin walked over, picked it up, dusted it off and handed it back to the teacher. Some boys laughed. He didn't seem to care. I don't know what he was feeling, but he looked proud.

qa.q: What did Zubin pick up after the anthem?
qa.a: One of the small paper flags.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been feeling during the anthem?
qa.a: He seemed proud and respectful, taking the moment seriously.

qa.q: How could the teacher respond to Zubin picking up the flag?
qa.a: Thank him quietly and use it to remind the class why the flag is treated with respect.

qa.q: How might Raghav see Zubin after the boys laughed?
qa.a: Raghav seems a bit impressed that Zubin didn't care about the laughter.

grounding: Shows a child honouring the anthem and flag at a school assembly, seen by a classmate.

passage: Two weeks before Republic Day: Gopika, ten, was bored at parade practice. "Why do we march for a day off?" she asked her brother Karthik. One week before: her teacher read the Preamble aloud and explained that it was a promise to every citizen. Gopika copied it neatly into her notebook. Republic Day: she marched in the front row, arms swinging. That afternoon she stuck the Preamble on the fridge and read it to Karthik, who rolled his eyes but listened.

qa.q: What did Gopika stick on the fridge?
qa.a: The Preamble.

qa.q: How did Gopika's feelings about Republic Day change?
qa.a: She went from bored to proud once she understood what the Preamble promised.

qa.q: What helped Gopika's attitude change?
qa.a: Her teacher explaining the meaning behind the day, not just the marching.

qa.q: What is it like for Karthik when Gopika reads the Preamble to him?
qa.a: He acts bored but listens, maybe a bit curious about his sister's new pride.

grounding: Shows a child moving from boredom to respect for a national day as she learns its meaning.

passage: "Hemant, you ask why I always fold the flag carefully. When I, your Nilesh Dada, was ten, our village school got its first proper flagpole. On Independence Day the headmaster chose me to pull the rope. I was so nervous that the flag got stuck halfway. Everyone was watching. My ears were burning. The headmaster walked over, calmly untangled it, and let me finish. Afterwards he showed me how to fold it, corner to corner, and said, 'We don't just own this. We look after it.' I've never forgotten."

qa.q: What did the headmaster choose Nilesh to do?
qa.a: To pull the rope.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel when the flag got stuck halfway?
qa.a: He felt nervous and embarrassed, with everyone watching.

qa.q: What turning point in the story shaped Nilesh's respect for the flag?
qa.a: The headmaster calmly helping him finish and then teaching him to fold it carefully.

qa.q: How might the headmaster have seen the stuck flag?
qa.a: As a chance to teach respect and care rather than as a failure.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child he learned to honour the flag and school ceremonies.

passage: I'm Kashish, from the flat below Vijay's. The morning after Holi, the colony park was a mess: colour packets, broken water balloons, paper cups. Vijay, who's eleven, came down with a bag and gloves and started picking up. Nobody asked him. Then he posted in the colony chat group, politely: "Park cleanup at ten, bring a bag if you can 🙂" He didn't blame anyone. By eleven, eight kids had joined. I don't know what made him do it, but he seemed happy when it was clean.

qa.q: What did Vijay bring down to the park?
qa.a: A bag and gloves.

qa.q: What might Vijay have been feeling when the park was clean?
qa.a: He seemed happy and satisfied that the community space was cared for.

qa.q: What did Vijay's message get right?
qa.a: It invited people politely without blaming anyone, so others felt welcome to join.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Vijay's actions?
qa.a: Kashish is impressed that he started without being asked, though not sure why he did it.

grounding: Shows a child taking ownership of a shared space and posting respectfully online, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Monday: someone in Class 5's chat group posted a mean photo of a classmate, Pooja, with a silly caption. Nandini, ten, saw it and felt sick, but did nothing. Wednesday: the photo was still being shared. Nandini didn't forward it. She messaged Pooja privately, "I'm sorry this is going round," and told her class teacher that afternoon. Friday: the teacher spoke to the class about kind posting. Nandini posted a drawing she'd made of the class tree instead, and Pooja reacted with a heart.

qa.q: What did Nandini message Pooja privately?
qa.a: "I'm sorry this is going round."

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when she first saw the photo?
qa.a: She felt sick and uncomfortable, knowing it was mean.

qa.q: What did Nandini do well by Wednesday?
qa.a: She didn't forward it, supported Pooja privately and told her teacher the same day.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel when Nandini messages her?
qa.a: Less alone and comforted that someone is on her side.

grounding: Shows a child taking responsibility for respectful behaviour online over a week.

passage: "You asked about the pond, Gurleen. When I, your Arnab Mama, was eleven, there was a small pond behind our house full of rubbish. Nobody cared. One summer I decided it was mine to look after. Every Sunday I pulled out bottles and plastic with a long stick. The neighbours laughed. Then one day a heron landed there. I ran to tell everyone. After that, the neighbours started helping, and the pond cleared. It wasn't anyone's job. But once I owned it, others did too."

qa.q: What landed at the pond one day?
qa.a: A heron.

qa.q: What was young Arnab feeling when the heron landed?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud that his cleaning had made a difference.

qa.q: What turning point in the story brought the neighbours in?
qa.a: The heron landing, which showed everyone the pond was worth saving.

qa.q: How might the neighbours have seen young Arnab at first?
qa.a: As a boy wasting his Sundays, until the heron changed their minds.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child he took ownership of a neglected community space.

passage: I'm Ganga, and I sit next to Asif in Class 10. After our chemistry test came back, he got 14 out of 40. I expected him to sulk. Instead, he spread the paper on his desk and wrote next to each wrong answer: "Knew it, misread," "Didn't know," "Panicked, skipped." Then he counted. Most were "Panicked, skipped." He muttered, "So it's not that I don't know it. It's that I freeze." He asked our teacher for practice papers with a timer. I'm not sure what he felt, but he looked more determined than upset.

qa.q: What mark did Asif get in the chemistry test?
qa.a: 14 out of 40.

qa.q: What does Asif muttering "It's that I freeze" suggest about his thinking?
qa.a: He felt relieved and more hopeful, realising his problem was panic, not lack of knowledge.

qa.q: Why is Asif's plan to practise with a timer a good next step?
qa.a: It targets the real flaw he found in his own thinking, freezing under time pressure.

qa.q: How does Ganga see Asif's reaction?
qa.a: Ganga expected sulking and is surprised he looked more determined than upset.

grounding: Shows a teenager analysing his own test mistakes to find the flaw in how he thinks under pressure, seen by a classmate.

passage: Week one: Anirban, fourteen, lost the school debate. He blamed the judges. His teammate Pema said, "You talked over the other side's last point." He shrugged. Week two: he lost again, and this time he asked Pema to record him. Listening back, he winced: he hadn't answered one argument, just spoken louder. Week three: he lost a practice round but noticed, halfway through, that he was rushing again, and made himself breathe before answering. Week four: he kept a small notebook during the debate, writing each opponent's point before replying. When Pema passed him a note saying "slow", he nodded. He won. That night he wrote in the same notebook: "I think better when I slow down my own head. My first answer is usually my loudest, not my best."

qa.q: What did Anirban ask Pema to do in week two?
qa.a: To record him.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he listened to the recording?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and uncomfortable, seeing that he hadn't really answered the other side.

qa.q: What small step changed his results?
qa.a: Writing down each opponent's point before replying, so he thought before he spoke.

qa.q: How might Pema see Anirban's change?
qa.a: She probably feels pleased and relieved that he took her feedback seriously.

grounding: Shows a teenager over a month learning to notice and fix flaws in his own thinking during debates.

passage: "Tushar, sit. You think you're bad at studying? When I, your Jahnavi Bua, was sixteen, I used to read my history notes three times and still forget everything. I thought I was stupid. One night I asked myself: what am I actually doing when I read? And I realised I was just moving my eyes, thinking about other things. So I tried closing the book and writing what I remembered, then checking. It was painful. I remembered almost nothing at first. But it showed me the truth about my own mind. My marks rose after that."

qa.q: How many times did young Jahnavi read her history notes?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: How did young Jahnavi feel before she changed her method?
qa.a: She felt stupid and frustrated that reading so much wasn't working.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Jahnavi studied?
qa.a: Asking herself what she was actually doing when she read, and testing herself instead.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi's teachers have seen the change in her marks?
qa.a: They would likely be pleased and curious about what she had changed.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager she learned to think about her own thinking and fix her study method.

passage: "Jomon, you asked how I knew to move the grain before the flood. When I, your Gautam Appachan, was fifteen, our village sat below the river bend. Everyone said, 'The river never comes this high.' But I sat on the bund and thought: what if it rains for five days, not two? What if the upstream dam opens? Where would the water go? I drew it in the mud with a stick. The low storeroom would flood first. So I talked my father into moving the sacks up to the loft. Two years later, the river came. Our grain was dry."

qa.q: Where did Gautam move the grain sacks to?
qa.a: Up to the loft.

qa.q: What was young Gautam feeling as he sat on the bund imagining floods?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and worried that the village was too sure the river would stay low.

qa.q: What turning point in the story saved the grain?
qa.a: Gautam playing out the what-if scenarios and persuading his father to move the sacks.

qa.q: How might Gautam's father have seen his son's idea at first?
qa.a: Maybe as overcautious, but he trusted him enough to act on it.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager he reasoned through what-if scenarios to prepare for a flood.

passage: The power went out the night before the board exam, and rumours flew through the colony chat group: the trains might be on strike tomorrow. Saurabh, sixteen, and his friend Harsha sat on the stairs with a torch. "Okay, what if the trains don't run?" Saurabh said. "Bus. What if the bus is packed?" "Auto from the station. What if we can't find one?" "We walk. It's forty minutes. So we leave at six." "And if there's no strike?" "Then we're early and bored." They set alarms and packed their hall tickets by torchlight.

qa.q: How long would the walk take?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What were Saurabh and Harsha feeling as they sat on the stairs?
qa.a: They were anxious about the exam and the possible strike, but calmer as they made a plan.

qa.q: What made their what-if planning useful?
qa.a: They followed each scenario to a backup and picked one clear plan: leave at six.

qa.q: What would change if they had just hoped the trains would run?
qa.a: They might have panicked in the morning with no plan if the strike happened.

grounding: Shows teenagers playing out several what-if scenarios to plan for an uncertain exam morning.

passage: In the Class 10 debate club in Bengaluru, the topic was: "What if school started at eleven?" Hansa, fifteen, pushed her glasses up her nose and took the "for" side. "Teenagers would sleep more, so they'd concentrate better." Neelam countered, "But then school ends at six. What about sports? And parents' office hours?" Hansa paused. "Then sports move to the morning. And what if parents could drop kids at ten-thirty on their way to work?" "What if they start work at nine?" Neelam asked. They kept going, each what-if opening another, until the bell rang and neither had won. On the way out, Hansa was still scribbling what-ifs on her hand.

qa.q: What was the debate topic?
qa.a: "What if school started at eleven?"

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she paused?
qa.a: She was probably thrown for a moment and uncertain, then eager to find a new answer.

qa.q: What could Hansa try to strengthen her argument?
qa.a: Map out each what-if on paper, including the problems, before the next debate.

qa.q: How might Neelam see the debate that no one won?
qa.a: As a fun challenge, enjoying how each question led to another.

grounding: Shows teenagers asking what-if questions and playing out a scenario that hasn't happened.

passage: In their village, Pooja, fifteen, was helping her father Kamal decide what to do about the yellowing cotton. "Use more fertilizer," the shopkeeper had said. Pooja frowned. "But Papa, it's rained for two weeks. The roots might be waterlogged. More fertilizer might wash into the canal. And the neighbour's field didn't turn yellow, and he has better drains." She sketched it in her notebook: rain, drains, roots, fertilizer, canal, arrows everywhere. Kamal looked at it for a long time. "So first we fix the drain." "And ask the agriculture officer," Pooja said. "Before we spend anything." Kamal folded the page and put it in his shirt pocket.

qa.q: What had the shopkeeper told them to use?
qa.a: More fertilizer.

qa.q: What was Pooja thinking when she frowned at the shopkeeper's advice?
qa.a: She was doubtful and uneasy, sensing that the problem involved more than just fertilizer.

qa.q: Which choice made sense, and why?
qa.a: Fixing the drain and asking the agriculture officer, because it addressed the whole system, not one part.

qa.q: How might Kamal see his daughter's sketch?
qa.a: With surprise and respect, seeing connections he hadn't put together.

grounding: Shows a teenager understanding how rain, drainage, roots and fertilizer interact on a farm.

passage: In Osaka, Hiroshi, sixteen, was annoyed that the school bus was always late. He and his friend Oskar decided to find out why. They timed the bus for a week and made a chart. It was late on days when the market opened, because delivery trucks blocked the road. It was also late on rainy days, when more parents drove. And since school started at the same time as the office rush, the traffic was worst then. Oskar said, "So it's not the driver." "It's everything together," Hiroshi said. They sent their chart to the school office with a suggestion: start ten minutes later.

qa.q: What blocked the road on market days?
qa.a: Delivery trucks.

qa.q: What might Hiroshi have felt when he saw the pattern in their chart?
qa.a: He probably felt satisfied and a bit surprised, realising the lateness came from many causes.

qa.q: What makes their suggestion to the school sensible?
qa.a: It targets one variable they can change, the start time, within the whole system.

qa.q: How might the bus driver see their findings?
qa.a: Relieved that someone noticed the delays weren't the driver's fault.

grounding: Shows teenagers working out how several separate factors combine to make a bus late.

passage: The school canteen queue was always chaos at lunch. Trisha, fourteen, and Siddharth were on the student council and decided to figure out why. They stood by the counter with a notebook. Two bells rang at the same time, so everyone arrived together. The popular samosas sold out first, so people rushed. Only one cashier was open. "If we change one thing, does it fix it?" Siddharth asked. Trisha tapped her pen against her chin, then drew circles and arrows. "If we stagger the bells, the rush spreads out. Then one cashier is enough." They took the diagram to the principal.

qa.q: How many cashiers were open?
qa.a: Only one cashier was open.

qa.q: What might Trisha have been feeling as she drew the circles and arrows?
qa.a: She seemed curious and absorbed, excited to see how the pieces fit together.

qa.q: Why is staggering the bells a smart first step?
qa.a: It changes the variable that drives the others, the rush, so the rest of the system copes.

qa.q: How might the principal see the students' diagram?
qa.a: With interest, maybe impressed that they looked at the whole system, not just blamed the cashier.

grounding: Shows teenagers mapping how bells, food choices and staff interact to cause a canteen rush.

passage: I'm Madhav. In Class 11 a new boy, Sumit, joined from Delhi. He spoke fast, used big words, and answered first in every class. I decided in two days that he was arrogant. Everything he did after that seemed to prove it. Then we were put together for a chemistry project. At my house, he admitted he talked fast because he was nervous in new places. I realised I'd only noticed things that fit my first idea. I'd made up my mind and then collected evidence. Now I try to wait a week before I judge anyone.

qa.q: Where did Sumit join from?
qa.a: From Delhi.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel on realising the judgement about Sumit was wrong?
qa.a: Madhav felt embarrassed and humbled, seeing that the first idea had shaped everything noticed after.

qa.q: What would you advise Madhav for meeting new people?
qa.a: Keep waiting before judging, and look for evidence that could prove the first impression wrong.

qa.q: How might Sumit have felt in those first days at the new school?
qa.a: Nervous and out of place, even while seeming confident.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising confirmation bias in a snap judgement about a new classmate.

passage:
Debate coach's note, Harish, January
Sabina (16) argued this week that exams should be scrapped. In the rebuttal, she said, "Everyone I know hates exams, so they're bad." Then she stopped mid-sentence and said, "Actually, that's just my feeling. I need evidence." The room went quiet. She asked for a minute, then argued from research on stress and learning instead. I told her afterwards that catching her own emotional reasoning mid-debate was the best moment of the session. I'm adding a short bias-spotting exercise to next week's practice, and I've asked Sabina to lead the first round.

qa.q: What did Sabina argue should be scrapped?
qa.a: Exams.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: She was probably unsettled and a bit embarrassed, realising her point rested on feeling, not evidence.

qa.q: Why is Harish's bias-spotting exercise a good next step?
qa.a: It helps the whole team practise catching emotional reasoning the way Sabina did.

qa.q: How might the other debaters see Sabina's moment?
qa.a: They might respect her honesty and feel encouraged to check their own reasoning.

grounding: Shows a teenager catching her own emotional reasoning mid-debate, noted by her coach.

passage:
Usha's diary, Thursday
Today I fought with Minakshi about a message going round the class group saying the board exams were cancelled. I was so sure it was true. I even argued with her in front of everyone. Then she asked, "Where did it come from?" I didn't know. I checked the board's website, and there was nothing. I believed it because I wanted it to be true. That's embarrassing to write. Minakshi was kind about it. Tomorrow I'll say sorry. Rule for me: if I really want something to be true, check it twice.

qa.q: What did the message claim?
qa.a: That the board exams were cancelled.

qa.q: How did Usha feel after checking the website?
qa.a: Usha felt embarrassed and humbled, seeing that wanting it to be true had clouded her judgement.

qa.q: What could Usha do before believing the next forwarded message?
qa.a: Check where it came from and look at the official source first.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel when Usha says sorry?
qa.a: Relieved and respected, glad their friendship survived the argument.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising that her wishes shaped her belief in a rumour.
